podcast.body: This anti-Nixon song was written by Neil Young in approximately an hour after seeing a Life magazine photo spread of the Kent State shootings. It specifically named Richard Nixon, linking him to the May 4, 1970, shooting of unarmed students by the Ohio National Guard. David Crosby, Graham Nash, and the band quickly assembled in Los Angeles to record it, and Atlantic Records head Ahmet Ertegun ensured its release within 10 days, packaged with the First Amendment text. While banned by many AM stations, it was played on FM radio, which catered to college students. "Ohio was a response to the Ohio National Guard shooting 12 unarmed students on the campus of Kensington University on May 4, 1970."

This protest song was written and performed by the group, including Neil Young, as a response to the 1970 violence at Kent State. It is noted as barely qualifying as a diss record because its songwriter, Neil Young, explicitly calls out President Richard Nixon by name. "Crosby Stills' Nash and Young's Ohio, a protest against the 1970 violence at Kent State barely qualifies as a disc record since songwriter Neil Young calls out President Richard Nixon by name."

podcast.body: This song is considered the centerpiece of the so-called Kent State songs. Neil Young wrote it within 15 minutes at a friend's house in Utano Canyon, California, after seeing a May 15th edition of Life Magazine featuring a photograph of 14-year-old Marianne Vecchio kneeling over the body of Jeff Miller, one of the students killed at Kent State. David Crosby witnessed its creation and immediately called Graham Nash to book studio time, prioritizing its release over the band's climbing hit "Teach Your Children." "I watched him write Ohio right there."
